newsitem.title: USA: Group says Ill. tollway extension to run deficit.
newsitem.headline: Group says Ill. tollway extension to run deficit.

text.p: A Chicago-based environmental group this week said that a planned bond-financed tollway extension in northeastern Illinois will not generate enough toll revenues to cover debt service.

A financial analysis by the Environmental Law & Policy Center indicated a proposed north extension of Illinois Highway 53 north would only cover 29 percent of the annual debt service needed for the estimated $1 billion project.

The group said the 20-mile tollroad would only generate $22 million a year in revenues, while projected debt service on $1 billion of 25-year bonds sold at an interest rate of 6.05 percent would be $78 million annually.
The remaining $56 million would have to come from tolls paid by motorists using existing tollroads, the group said.

David Loveday, spokesman for the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority, said the agency was still in the process of drafting an environmental impact statement for the project and had not done any cost analysis at this time.
"We have not gotten that far yet," Loveday said.

Earlier this year, the environmental group released a financial analysis of the authority's planned south extension of I-355 into Will County. That analysis found a $40 million annual shortfall in revenues to cover debt service on the nearly $700 million of bonds expected to be issued for that project.
Loveday said the authority has anticipated a $40 million shortfall annual revenue shortfall for the south I-355 extension that would be made up for with revenues from existing tollroads.

In addition to the financial analyses, the environmental group and others filed a lawsuit last month in U.S. District Court in Chicago seeking an injunction against construction of the south extension. The lawsuit claimed the environmental impact statement for the project was flawed.
Loveday said the first bond issue for the south I-355 extension, which got the green light from Gov. Jim Edgar last month, would be sold late this year or early next year.
